title: Who Owns the Bank: The Rise and Fall of Black-Owned Banks | At The Margins, Ep. 3
lede: Black Americans founded 134 banks between 1888 and 1934. By 2021, 18 Black-owned banks held about 0.02% of U.S. bank assets. Episode 3 of At The Margins follows the money through Black-owned banks and credit unions in the U.S. and Canada: why they disappeared, where they lend, the 2020 rush of deposits and public capital, this year's merger and rule change, and what the evidence says works.
keyPoints: Black-owned banks fell from 48 in 2001 to 18 in 2021, with $5.35B in combined assets vs $23.7T for all U.S. banks (Chicago Fed; Berger et al.; FDIC).

Minority-owned banks made ~15% of their mortgages in majority-Black neighborhoods vs 1–3% for other banks; 48% of Black MDI mortgages in 2019–22 went to Black borrowers (Chicago Fed; NBA Foundation researchers).
Treasury's ECIP put $1.4B into Black-owned and Black-majority institutions; Optus Bank went from ~$1M a month in loans to $30M+ in four weeks (U.S. Treasury).
Optus–M&F merger (~$1.27B, pending) would create the largest African American-owned financial institution; the OCC narrowed its MDI policy in June 2026 (National Bankers Association).
Canada: three Black-owned credit unions in Ontario closed by 1995; the Pan-African Credit Union is seeking a license (PACU; TMU Diversity Institute).
